text: You already know Install-Module Az and Connect-AzAccount from earlier in this path. This lesson goes deeper: what Az actually installs underneath the hood, how to sign a script in to Azure without a human sitting there to click through a browser prompt, and why keeping the module updated is an automation concern, not just routine housekeeping.

Az isn't one module — it's an umbrella over dozens of smaller, service-specific sub-modules. Get-AzVM lives in Az.Compute. Get-AzStorageAccount lives in Az.Storage. Get-AzSqlDatabase lives in Az.Sql. Running Get-Module -Name Az.* -ListAvailable shows the whole family installed on a machine, one entry per Azure service area, each with its own version number. A runbook that only ever touches virtual machines and resource groups really only depends on Az.Accounts, Az.Compute, and Az.Resources — not the entire umbrella it happened to install alongside.

Connect-AzAccount by itself opens an interactive browser sign-in — useless inside a script running unattended at 2 a.m. with nobody watching. Azure PowerShell authenticates as a service principal instead: an application identity rather than a person. The app ID becomes the credential's username, a client secret becomes the password, and Connect-AzAccount -ServicePrincipal signs the session in with no browser window and no one around to approve it.

Azure ships new features and occasional breaking changes constantly, and the Az module tracks that pace with frequent releases, each one documented in its own changelog that calls out exactly what changed. Get-InstalledModule -Name Az shows what version is on the machine right now. Update-Module -Name Az pulls the newest release down from the PowerShell Gallery. Checking a single sub-module's version afterward confirms the update actually landed — not optional hygiene for anything that runs unattended on a fixed schedule with nobody reading the console output.

Next: looping over Azure resources with PowerShell — using Get-AzVM piped into a foreach loop to check and act on every virtual machine in a subscription at once, instead of one VM typed by hand at a time.
